name: ESP32-2432S024N (Cheap Yellow Display, 2.4in, N variant)
summary: The tightest board penguinOS runs on, and the one that sets tier 0. Also sold as HW-950, which is the marking on the silkscreen and the only identifier the board carries. Written from documentation long before any unit was on a bench, and VERIFIED on hardware afterwards: every display pin, the backlight, the wire format, the channel order, the orientation and the heap all came back as described. The one thing documentation could not have told us is that its controller answers no ID register at all - 0x04, 0xD3 and 0xB6 all read zero - so the panel had to be identified by how it BEHAVES rather than by what it says it is.

render.reason: MEASURED BY penguinOS ITSELF, not by a probe, and the distinction is the whole point of this field. A bare bring-up probe on this board reports free=281612 / largest=147456; penguinOS at app_main reports free=148188 / largest=110592. The difference is the OS's own static footprint, and a budget taken from the probe is not a budget the OS can ever honour. Recording the probe figure here made the display backend size its strips at 293 rows and ask heap_caps_malloc for 281,280 contiguous DMA bytes out of a 110,592-byte largest block; it failed with EOS_ERR_POOL and the board booted blind. band_height 40 and full_framebuffer false follow from the same measurement: two 40-row strips at 240 wide is 38,400 bytes, which fits the largest block with room left for Wi-Fi, NimBLE, the web server and the buddy. A full 240x320 frame would need 153,600 bytes for one and 307,200 for the two the backend double-buffers - more than this board's entire free heap. That is what keeps it at tier 0, and the number that decides it is the largest BLOCK, never the free total.

display.pixel_format_reason: RGB565 straight down the wire, two bytes per pixel.
display.clock_reason: 40MHz is the rate the proven cyd24 firmware runs. MISO is bound on this board (GPIO12) because the module wires it, and a bound MISO caps what the ESP32 SPI driver will actually clock, so 80MHz would not be honoured even if the panel tolerated it. Do not raise this without re-testing the whole panel, not just a test card.
display.byte_swap_reason: VERIFIED on hardware, together with color_order, by a three-primary test - the only instrument that separates them. Byte order and channel order are NOT independently observable with one colour, and they are barely observable with gold: under swap+BGR #d4af37 lands on a yellow-green that reads as 'yellowish gold' and cheerfully confirms the wrong model, which is exactly what happened here for several rounds. Driving the panel in RGB order and storing 0xF800, 0x07E0, 0x001F as three full-width bands makes each of the four models produce a DIFFERENT sequence: R,G,B is no-swap+RGB; B,G,R is no-swap+BGR; B,R,G is swap+RGB; R,B,G is swap+BGR. The panel showed RED, BLUE, GREEN - swap+BGR, with no arithmetic required of anyone.
display.mirror_reason: VERIFIED true on X, and this board is exactly why mirror_x/mirror_y exist. The bring-up probe never CALLED esp_lcd_panel_mirror at all, so it inherited whatever MADCTL the esp_lcd ILI9341 init left behind - and its two Fs, one as stored and one pre-mirrored, showed the as-stored one reading correctly. penguinOS is not so passive: rotation 0 makes it call mirror(false, false) explicitly, which CLEARS the MX bit the driver's own default had set, and the whole screen came up mirrored - the QR code and every word backwards. mirror_x true XORs that bit back on. The lesson generalises past this board: a probe that omits a call is not testing the same configuration as an OS that makes it with default arguments. Handedness is invisible in every log and every colour test, so it can only be caught by drawing something asymmetric AND driving the panel the way the OS will - a QR code nobody can scan is the failure mode.
display.invert_reason: VERIFIED false. Inversion never had to be guessed at here: the three-primary test returned saturated primaries in a recognisable permutation, and an inverting panel would have returned their complements - cyan, yellow, magenta - which is not a result anyone can mistake for red, blue and green.
display.offset_reason: VERIFIED zero. A 240-wide fill reached both edges with no shear and no black column, and the row-count test placed row 0 at the top of the glass.

bluetooth_keyboard.reason: NimBLE is 19KB of heap; Bluedroid is 83KB, which is instant OOM on a board with 20KB free. Release classic-BT memory and bring BLE up BEFORE WiFi, then WiFi.setSleep(true). The K809 keyboard bonds to whichever board it paired with last.

bad_baud_rates.reason: Fails within a second of 'Configuring flash size...' with "A fatal error occurred: Invalid head of packet (0xFD): Possible serial noise or corruption." - the byte differs run to run (0xFD, 0x7D seen). Reproduced on a 64 KB read, so it is not a length effect: 460800 simply does not work on this CH340. 230400 passes the same read every time.

panel_id_register.note: Not attempted. The ILI9488 boards proved that a controller ID read is not something to build on, so nothing in penguinOS reads one.

distinguishing_notes: 2.4 inch panel in a yellow PCB with a microSD slot on the left edge.
Silkscreened ESP32-2432S024N, sometimes HW-950. The trailing N is the variant letter and the only thing separating it from the R variant, which does have an XPT2046 touch chip.
CH340 bridge, so it enumerates as /dev/cu.usbserial-* rather than a native USB device.
identification.confirm_prompt: Is this the 2.4in Cheap Yellow Display, and does the silkscreen end in N rather than R? The R variant has touch and this profile does not configure it.

gotchas.text: There is no touch controller. Every input path has to come from the BLE keyboard, the BOOT button, USB serial or the board's own web page.
Bluedroid does not fit. 83KB against 19KB for NimBLE, on a board with about 20KB free at steady state. Linking Bluedroid gives an out-of-memory crash during BLE init, not a subtle degradation.
Release classic-BT memory and initialise BLE before WiFi. The other order leaves the heap too fragmented for the BLE allocation to land.
The RGB LED is active low. Pins left as inputs or driven high are off; the naive all-pins-high-is-white assumption gives you a permanently white LED.
About 20KB free heap at steady state with WiFi and BLE up. Any new subsystem has to be measured against that, not estimated.
Panel is on HSPI and the microSD is on VSPI (SCK18 MISO19 MOSI23 CS5). They do not share a bus, so no bus lock is needed between them.

MISO is wired on GPIO12 and WORKS - 0x09 (RDDST) returns 00 30 80 00 00 and 0x0A (RDDPM) returns 08 00, real data - but every identification register reads zero: 0x04 RDDID, 0xD3 RDID4 and 0xB6 Display Function Control all come back 00 00 00 00. So a read of zeros here does NOT mean the pins are wrong, and a probe that concludes that will send you looking for a wiring fault that does not exist. It also closes off the neatest way to measure resolution: 0xB6's NL field would have given the line count directly. Identify this panel by behaviour instead - see the two gotchas below.

The two axes fail DIFFERENTLY when you paint past the panel, and knowing which is which is what makes the resolution measurable without a datasheet. Painting 320 columns wide SHEARS: the controller clamps its column window to 239 and each row's surplus 80 pixels spill into the next row, stepping the whole image diagonally. Painting 480 rows tall does NOT shear - the row counter clamps at 319 and every remaining row lands on top of row 319, so 80 rows of white collapse into a ONE-PIXEL HAIRLINE at the bottom edge. A hairline where a band was expected is the signature of a 320-row panel, and it is easy to misread as 'the band is there, so the panel is taller'. Test height with the width pinned to a value both candidates accept, or the shear makes the result unreadable.

460800 fails outright - 'Invalid head of packet', within a second - so it is listed in bad_baud_rates and upload_baud drops to 230400. But baud is only half the story and the more useful half is this: at 230400 a 64 KB read succeeds every time while a continuous 4 MB read dies around 52% with 'Corrupt data, expected 0x1000 bytes but received 0xfa7'. The corruption is a function of read LENGTH, not rate. Back this board up in 512 KB chunks with a retry around each and concatenate them; all eight chunks then pass first time. backup/factory-4MB.bin was captured that way, sha256 81cff512b796c94ce16dc0b9fac0c13fe4d858367f5918b7740ebc934bb4cc5b.

VERIFIED by asking the chip. This profile previously said no touch controller was fitted, from a 60-second probe that found nothing. That probe was not careless - it was testing the wrong hypothesis. Every community source for this family puts touch on a SEPARATE SPI bus (25/32/39, or 22/26/39), and BOTH of those are genuinely empty here: all four XPT2046 channels return an identical 0 on each. The chip is on the PANEL'S OWN BUS - sclk 14, mosi 13, miso 12 - with only CS on its own pin at 33. The discriminator is variation, not magnitude. Untouched, the part answers Z1=2 and Z2=4064/4062/4047; that three-count wobble is real converter noise and a floating MISO cannot produce it, while the empty buses return the same value every time. Pressure is the Z1/Z2 ratio, so Z1 near zero against Z2 near full scale is the correct no-finger reading. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DRIVER: touch shares SPI2 with the display, so every poll must take the panel's bus lock - the same constraint peripherals.sdcard records with shares_display_bus, and a tighter one, because the panel is mid-band far more often than the card is mid-read. A touch poll that barges in during a band write tears the picture. Clock the XPT2046 at 1-2 MHz; it does not tolerate the panel's 40 MHz.
